source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
finding: An LLM reasons offline about a context before any question arrives, writes a richer re-represented context, and answers faster later. This is Dyna-style offline simulation done in text.
numbers: About 5x less test-time compute for the same accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME. Scaling sleep-time compute adds up to +13% (GSM) and +18% (AIME) accuracy. Models: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, o1, o3-mini, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek-R1; o1 showed limited gains.
limits: Only two phases (sleep, test). Benchmarks are synthetic splits of existing math sets. Gain depends on the query being predictable from the context.
agent_relevance: Direct template for offline replay that updates a subgoal library: precompute likely sub-questions and lemmas, store them, retrieve at decision time.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute, Multi-Query and amortisation result
finding: Sharing one offline pass across several questions on the same context lowers cost per query. With few questions per context, sleep-time compute is not worth its cost.
numbers: Average cost per query falls 2.5x on Multi-Query GSM-Symbolic when amortised (1, 2, 5, 10 questions per context tested; gain grows with the number).
limits: Cost advantage only when questions per context are many. Cost measured with API prices in the paper's own model.
agent_relevance: Replay pays off when a stored subgoal is reused many times; gate offline replay on expected reuse count.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute, predictability analysis
finding: Examples were binned into five groups by how predictable the question is from the context (scored by a language model log-probability). The accuracy gain from sleep-time over test-time compute rose with predictability.
numbers: Five predictability quantiles on Stateful GSM-Symbolic P1 and P2 with GPT-4o-mini; gain largest in the most predictable bins. Sleep-time also beat parallel pass@k at equal test-time tokens.
quote: sleep-time compute is most effective when the queries are predictable from the context
limits: Predictability proxy comes from one small model; correlation not given as a single number in the text I read.
agent_relevance: This is the LLM analogue of replay prioritisation (need/gain): spend offline compute where the future query is predictable.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute, SWE-Features agentic case study
finding: In a multi-file feature task the agent explores the repository offline. At low test-time budgets this gives higher F1 on the set of files to modify. At high budgets plain test-time compute wins.
numbers: Metric: F1 of predicted vs true modified-file set; model Claude 3.7 Sonnet; test-time budgets about 3000-10000 tokens. Sleep-time agent edited more files, lower precision.
limits: No unit tests, only file-set F1. Single model. Reversal at high budgets is a boundary condition.
agent_relevance: Offline replay can lead to over-editing; keep a precision check when stored knowledge drives actions.

source: Yu et al. (2025) Dyna-Think: Synergizing Reasoning, Acting, and World Model Simulation in AI Agents
finding: Named after Dyna. Trains a 32B model to simulate next states inside its reasoning (R1 reasoning reduced to simulation), then trains world model and policy together (DDT).
numbers: OSWorld (174 tasks, 3 runs), Qwen2.5-32B base: avg success 14.2 -> 26.6 (DDT with critique), best-of-N 27.0 -> 44.3. R1 (685B) prompted: 31.2 avg, 44.8 BoN. DIT(R1)+RFT: 23.2 / 38.5. About 2x fewer generated tokens than R1.
limits: Trained, not scaffold-only. Avg success still below R1 (26.6 vs 31.2). Evaluation on computer-use tasks; world-model accuracy judged by GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Best-of-N parity with a much bigger model suggests that simulating next states beats longer thinking; a scaffold could ask for a short next-state prediction before each action.

source: Yu et al. (2025) Dyna-Think, vanilla Dyna ablation and WindowsAgentArena
finding: Classic Dyna (plan with a separately trained world model) helped little on OSWorld and hurt on a second benchmark. Training the model to be its own world model with next-state or critique targets worked better.
numbers: OSWorld avg: RFT 23.2, +vanilla Dyna 23.2 (BoN 38.5), +DDT critique 26.6 (BoN 44.3). WindowsAgentArena avg: R1 26.9, DIT+RFT 28.4, +vanilla Dyna 20.9, +DDT next-state 34.9, +DDT critique 32.8.
limits: Three runs; standard deviations about 1-2 points. Different training set sizes per method.
agent_relevance: A separate learned simulator can be worse than none; ground simulation in the same model and check it against outcomes.

source: Yu et al. (2025) Dyna-Think, world-model accuracy vs task success
finding: Models that simulate next states more accurately also succeed more. DDT training raised world-model accuracy with the same policy data as RFT.
numbers: Per-task correlation between world-model accuracy and success: r at least 0.32 across all models (minimum). DDT raised world-model accuracy by 16.8 points absolute over RFT. Accuracy judged by GPT-4o on turns up to 30 steps.
limits: Correlational. LLM judge for accuracy. Pearson r on per-task averages.
agent_relevance: Supports logging prediction-vs-outcome per step as a cheap signal of when simulation can be trusted.

source: Gu et al. (2024) Is Your LLM Secretly a World Model of the Internet? (WebDreamer)
finding: Before acting, the LLM imagines the outcome of each candidate action in text and scores it. This replaces real tree search with simulated lookahead.
numbers: Success %, reactive vs WebDreamer(GPT-4o): VisualWebArena 17.6 vs 23.6 (+34.1% rel), Online-Mind2Web 26.0 vs 37.0 (+42.3%), Mind2Web-Live 20.2 vs 25.0 (+23.8%). Real tree search on VWA: 26.2.
limits: Still below real tree search on VWA (23.6 vs 26.2). Simulation errors on unfamiliar sites. Tree search impossible on live sites.
agent_relevance: Cheap simulated lookahead gets most of the gain of real search. Good model for the offline-rehearsal step.

source: Gu et al. (2024) WebDreamer efficiency and world-model choice
finding: Simulation costs far less than real exploration. A small fine-tuned world model nearly matches GPT-4o.
numbers: Steps (GPT-4o): reactive 3.4-5.1, tree search 9.9-13.6, WebDreamer 4.1-5.2. Wall-clock seconds: reactive 68-88, tree search 749-972, WebDreamer 180-234 (4-5x faster than tree search). Dreamer-7B: VWA 21.9, Mind2Web 35.0, Live 24.0; vanilla Qwen2-VL-7B: 17.2, 31.0, 19.2.
limits: Fine-tuned model trained on synthetic data from this paper's pipeline. Single-run percentages on small sets.
agent_relevance: Offline simulation can be done by a small cheaper model while a big model acts.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Can Language Models Serve as Text-Based World Simulators?
finding: GPT-4 is an unreliable simulator of state changes in text games. Errors concentrate on arithmetic, common-sense and scientific properties.
numbers: Accuracy does not exceed 59.9% for transitions with a non-trivial state change. In the parsed text GPT-4 reaches at best 77.1% on dynamic action-driven and at most 49.7% on environment-driven transitions (two-column text; check original). Game progress: 92.1% with rules in context, 61.5% without. Humans 80% vs sampled GPT-4 50%. 2954 transition tuples.
limits: Only GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (2024). Text-game domain. Per-step errors compound over a rollout.
agent_relevance: Imagined rollouts drift. Replay built on LLM simulation needs outcome grounding and short horizons.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Scaling Agent Learning via Experience Synthesis (DreamGym)
finding: Agents are trained in an LLM-simulated environment with a replay buffer seeded by real data and a task curriculum. The replay buffer is a core part.
numbers: WebArena-Lite: over 30% better than all baselines. WebShop and ALFWorld: on par with GRPO/PPO trained on 80K real transitions with zero real interactions. Sim-to-real: over 40% gain with under 10% real data. Training effort one-third to one-fifth of RL baselines.
limits: Success rates on WebArena stay low (about 6-14%). Gains are on trained policies, not scaffolds. Backbones: Llama 3.2-3B, 3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B.
agent_relevance: Offline synthetic experience can replace real interaction for some learning; retrieval of similar past trajectories guides the simulator.

source: Chen et al. (2025) DreamGym ablation
finding: Removing the replay buffer, the reasoning trace in the experience model, or the task generator each lowers success.
numbers: Full DreamGym: WebShop 63.9, WebArena 13.3. Without experience replay: 59.2 and 9.7. Without experience reasoning: 55.8 and 7.3. Without task generation: 57.3 and 7.3 (drops of 6.6 and 6.0 points).
limits: One backbone in the ablation table as far as I could parse; single seeds not stated.
agent_relevance: Replay is necessary but a curriculum of new tasks is needed so the buffer does not saturate.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: The agent induces reusable workflows (routines) from past successful trajectories, offline or online, and puts them in memory. This is replay that updates a subgoal library.
numbers: WebArena (812 tasks, GPT-4): 35.5 total success vs 23.5 BrowserGym baseline (+12.0 points, +51.1% rel). Mind2Web: +24.6% rel step success. Fewer steps than baselines. Online gain over baseline grows from 8.9 to 14.0 points as train-test gap widens; up to 22.5 points after tens of examples.
limits: Workflows come only from successes judged by an evaluator. Abstract says +7.9% over human-written workflows (SteP); body says 7.6%.
agent_relevance: Closest existing match to our need: offline induction of subgoal templates from solved episodes, reused later.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: LLM acts as both world model and agent, with Monte Carlo tree search over simulated reasoning steps.
numbers: RAP on LLaMA-33B beats CoT on GPT-4 with 33% relative improvement in plan generation.
limits: Read arXiv abstract page only. Needs many LLM calls per problem.
agent_relevance: Imagined rollouts as search over reasoning; a costly cousin of Dyna planning.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) Evaluating Cognitive Maps and Planning in LLMs with CogEval
finding: Tested 8-10 LLMs on tasks taken from human cognitive-map experiments, including reward revaluation, transition revaluation, shortcut and detour. Found no emergent planning; failures were invalid trajectories and loops.
numbers: 30 responses per prompt, six graph structures, three domains. GPT-4 mean score: 1-step path 0.99, 2-step 0.82, 3-step 0.55, transition revaluation 0.60, detour 0.55, shortcut 0.56. Alpaca-7B 1-step 0.27. Logistic regression: detour coefficient -2.35, shortcut -2.01 (p<0.001).
quote: These findings do not support the idea of emergent out-of-the-box planning ability in LLMs.
limits: Text-only; human tasks were never linguistic. Score is a normalised measure (0 poor, 1 optimal). Models from 2023.
agent_relevance: Revaluation tasks are the tests SR-Dyna passes; LLMs fail them in plain prompting, so an explicit replay or graph-update step is needed.

source: Momennejad et al. (2023) CogEval, effect of chain-of-thought and BFS/DFS prompts
finding: Chain-of-thought and graph-search instructions (BFS, DFS) helped only a little and mostly on community-graph tasks. Some CoT shortcut cells were unstable.
numbers: Experiment 2 varied temperature 0, 0.5, 1 with Original, +BFS, +DFS prompts on cluster count, shortest path and cluster-path tasks; gains marginal. nonteleShortcutCoT scores of 1.00 for GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 reflect very few valid cells, per the table's zero SE.
limits: Small cell counts in CoT conditions. Not a controlled ablation of scaffold size.
agent_relevance: Prompt-level scaffolds alone do not give flexible re-planning; structural memory is needed.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Agent writes verbal reflections on failures into an episodic buffer and reuses them next trial. A text form of replay with no weight updates.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% vs 80% for GPT-4 baseline; gains also on sequential decision and reasoning tasks.
limits: Read arXiv abstract page only. Needs a feedback signal (tests or reward).
agent_relevance: Cheap post-episode replay: store a lesson per failure, retrieve by similarity.

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: Agent collects experiences on training tasks, distils natural-language insights and retrieves past successes at inference; performance rises as experience accumulates.
numbers: AAAI-24 paper; abstract reports gains with experience but gives no single headline number on the page.
limits: Read arXiv abstract page only. Numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Offline insight extraction from trajectories is a replay-and-consolidate loop without training.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents
finding: Memory stream plus periodic reflection that turns recent memories into higher-level insights, then retrieval for planning. Reflection is replay-like consolidation.
numbers: 25 agents; ablation shows observation, planning and reflection each add to believability.
limits: Read arXiv abstract page only. Human-rated believability, not task success.
agent_relevance: Reflection triggers on importance accumulation: a usable trigger for when to run offline replay.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager
finding: Growing library of verified code skills plus automatic curriculum; skills stored after success are reused and composed.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distances, tech-tree milestones up to 15.3x faster than prior best.
limits: Read arXiv abstract page only. Minecraft with GPT-4; no replay of failures beyond iterative prompting.
agent_relevance: Skill library with verification before storing is the subgoal-library design we want.

source: Schaul et al. (2016) Prioritized Experience Replay
finding: Replay transitions with large learning error more often. This is the deep-RL form of prioritised sweeping.
numbers: Beat uniform replay on 41 of 49 Atari games with DQN.
limits: Read arXiv abstract page only. Sampling bias needs correction; priorities can go stale.
agent_relevance: Prioritise replay by surprise (prediction error), not uniformly.

source: Andrychowicz et al. (2017) Hindsight Experience Replay
finding: Relabel failed episodes with the goal actually reached, so a failure becomes a success for a different goal.
numbers: Three robot tasks (push, slide, pick-and-place) learned from binary reward only; ablations show it is essential there.
limits: Read arXiv abstract page only. Needs goal-conditioned setting.
agent_relevance: Failed attempts can seed the subgoal library by relabelling what they did achieve.

source: Zhang and Sutton (2017) A Deeper Look at Experience Replay
finding: A large replay buffer can hurt. Proposes a simple O(1) fix (always include the newest transition).
numbers: Tested on grid world and Atari; abstract gives no numbers.
limits: Read arXiv abstract page only. Numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: old stored items can swamp fresh evidence; cap or age out the library.

source: Fedus et al. (2020) Revisiting Fundamentals of Experience Replay
finding: Larger replay capacity helps some algorithms and not others; uncorrected n-step returns helped most; replay ratio matters.
numbers: Abstract gives no figures.
limits: Read arXiv abstract page only. Numbers not read.
agent_relevance: How much to replay is an empirical knob, not free.

source: van Seijen and Sutton (2013) Planning by Prioritized Sweeping with Small Backups
finding: Small backups make each planning update cost independent of the number of successor states, improving prioritised sweeping.
numbers: Abstract: substantial improvement over classical implementations; no figures.
limits: Read arXiv abstract page only. Numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Keep each offline update tiny and local, so many can be run.

source: Hafner et al. (2023) Mastering Diverse Domains through World Models (DreamerV3)
finding: Learns a world model and trains behaviour on imagined rollouts; first to get diamonds in Minecraft from scratch.
numbers: One configuration over more than 150 tasks.
limits: Read arXiv abstract page only. Trained network, not a language scaffold.
agent_relevance: Evidence that planning in imagination scales when the model is accurate.

source: Russek et al. (2017) Predictive representations can link model-based RL to model-free mechanisms (SR-Dyna)
finding: SR-Dyna replays experience offline to update a successor matrix. With enough replay it passes reward, transition and policy revaluation; with little replay it falls back to SR-TD and passes only reward revaluation.
numbers: Policy revaluation simulation used 10,000 random replay samples. SR matrix has S^2 entries. Read first ~100,000 of 182,793 characters.
limits: Replay scheme naive; memory scales S^2; many animal detour results solvable by SR-TD; truly novel options need semantic knowledge.
agent_relevance: Replay amount sets which kinds of revaluation the library can handle; start with cheap random replay, add priority later.

source: Momennejad (2020) Learning structures: predictive representations, replay, and generalization
finding: Review linking SR, replay and generalisation; the same author later built CogEval. Not opened this session.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Recorded from memory of the reference list only.
agent_relevance: Bridge between human replay theory and the LLM tests.

source: Sutton (1991) Dyna, an integrated architecture for learning, planning, and reacting
finding: Original Dyna: interleave real experience with simulated experience from a learned model. Not opened this session.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Recorded from memory only.
agent_relevance: The template our loop copies: act, learn model, replay.

source: Moore and Atkeson (1993) Prioritized sweeping
finding: Updates states in order of how much their value is expected to change. Not opened this session.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Recorded from memory only.
agent_relevance: Priority queue for offline updates.
